questions.q: A farmer wants to divide his field into beds. He walks along the edge of the field and counts his steps. Which body-based unit of length is he using?
questions.a: Stride

questions.q: Sameer writes the length of a vegetable bed as '9 strides'. In this record, which part is the unit?
questions.a: stride

questions.q: (a) Name two parts of the body, other than the hand, that people have used to measure length. (b) Give one reason why such body-based units are not reliable.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: foot length, stride, arm length, fist, finger width. (b) They differ from person to person, so different people measuring the same length get different numbers.
s: (a) Names two body parts such as the foot, stride, arm, fist or finger
(b) States that these units differ from person to person, so results differ

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When five friends measured the same classroom table in handspans, they did not all get the same number.
Reason (R): The handspans of different people are of different sizes.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the units of length mentioned in ancient Indian literature?
questions.a: Kilometre

questions.q: Dadi measures the border of a new saree as 6 arm-lengths. Her granddaughter Nisha measures the same border as 8 arm-lengths. Both measured carefully, without gaps. (a) Whose arm is longer? Give a reason. (b) Nisha tells her friend, 'The border is 8 long.' What is missing from her statement? (c) What should the two of them use so that they get the same result?
questions.a: (a) Dadi's arm is longer: fewer of her arm-lengths fit along the same border, so each one must be longer. (b) The unit is missing; a length has a number and a unit, so she should say '8 arm-lengths'. (c) A standard unit such as the metre, using a metre scale or a measuring tape.
s: (a) Says Dadi's arm is longer because fewer arm-lengths cover the same border
(b) Says the unit is missing: a length needs a number and a unit
(c) Suggests a standard unit (metre/centimetre) with a metre scale or measuring tape

questions.q: Four children measure the width of the same classroom door by placing their fists side by side. They count 7, 8, 8 and 9 fists. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.a: The child who counted 9 fists has the smallest fist.
o: The child who counted 9 fists has the smallest fist.
The child who counted 9 fists has the largest fist.
The door is exactly 8 fists wide, as two children got 8.
The child who counted 7 fists must have counted wrongly.

questions.q: A ribbon seller at a weekly market in Surat sells ribbon 'by the arm-length'. Two customers each ask for 5 arm-lengths of ribbon. Asha's arm-length is 40 cm and Bhavna's is 48 cm. The seller's own arm-length is 45 cm. (a) If Asha and Bhavna each measure the ribbon with their own arm, how many centimetres does each get? (b) How many centimetres does a customer get if the seller measures with his own arm? (c) For the same '5 arm-lengths', how much more ribbon does Bhavna get than Asha when each uses her own arm? (d) Bhavna wants to use her own arm, but Asha wants the seller to use his arm. Explain why each prefers this. (e) Suggest a fair way to sell ribbon so that this dispute does not arise, and say why it works.
questions.a: (a) Asha: 5 x 40 = 200 cm; Bhavna: 5 x 48 = 240 cm. (b) 5 x 45 = 225 cm. (c) 240 - 200 = 40 cm more. (d) Bhavna gets 240 cm with her arm but only 225 cm with the seller's, so she prefers her own; Asha gets 225 cm with the seller's arm but only 200 cm with hers, so she prefers his. (e) Sell by a standard unit such as the metre, measured with a metre scale or measuring tape; it is the same for everyone, so every buyer of the same length gets the same ribbon.
s: (a) Finds 200 cm for Asha and 240 cm for Bhavna
(b) Finds 225 cm with the seller's arm
(c) Finds the difference of 40 cm
(d) Compares 240 with 225 and 200 with 225 to explain each customer's choice
(e) Suggests selling in metres/centimetres with a scale or tape because a standard unit does not change from person to person

questions.q:
In a school in Bikaner, five Class 6 students measure the length of the same notice board with their handspans. Their records are: Ravi, 9 handspans; Sita, slightly more than 9 handspans; Amar, 10 handspans; Noor, between 9 and 10 handspans; Gita, slightly less than 9 handspans. Each of them placed the handspans carefully, one after another, without gaps.
(a) Who recorded the largest number of handspans?
(b) Who recorded the smallest number of handspans?
(c) Why did the five students get different results for the same notice board?
(d) The teacher wants one result that every student will agree on. What should the class measure with, and why?
questions.a: (a) Amar (10 handspans). (b) Gita (slightly less than 9 handspans). (c) Their handspans are of different sizes; a handspan differs from person to person. (d) A metre scale or measuring tape marked in standard units (metre, centimetre), because a standard unit is the same for everyone, so all measurements of the board will agree.
s: (a) Names Amar
(b) Names Gita
(c) Explains that handspans differ in size from person to person
(d) Chooses a scale or tape in standard units and says a standard unit is the same for everyone

questions.q: True or False? 'The angula, a finger-width unit of length mentioned in ancient Indian literature, is still used by some craftspeople today.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The angula (finger width) is still used by traditional craftspeople such as carpenters and tailors.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: carpenters and tailors still use the angula (finger width)

questions.q: What is the SI unit of length?
questions.a: metre

questions.q: One lap of the running track in a stadium is 400 m long. What is this length in kilometres?
questions.a: 0.4 km

questions.q: (a) A pencil sharpener is 3 cm long. Write this length in millimetres. (b) A curtain is 2.5 m long. Write this length in centimetres.
s: (a) Uses 1 cm = 10 mm to get 30 mm
(b) Uses 1 m = 100 cm to get 250 cm

questions.q:
Match each length in Column I with the equal length in Column II.
Column I: I. 1 km  II. 1 m  III. 1 cm  IV. 1 inch
Column II: A. 10 mm  B. 100 cm  C. 1000 m  D. 2.54 cm
questions.a: I-C, II-B, III-A, IV-D

questions.q:
Read these statements about writing lengths.
I. The symbol for kilometre is written in lowercase letters as km.
II. A length of 5 metres is written as 5 ms, because it is more than one metre.
III. A space is left between the number and the unit, as in 12 cm.
Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only

questions.q: A gardener has a 10 m roll of wire. To tie up his plants he cuts 6 pieces that are each 1.25 m long and 4 pieces that are each 45 cm long. (a) What total length of wire, in centimetres, has he cut? (b) How many centimetres of wire are left on the roll? (c) Write the length that is left in metres and in millimetres.
questions.a: (a) 6 x 125 cm = 750 cm and 4 x 45 cm = 180 cm, so 930 cm in all. (b) 10 m = 1000 cm, so 1000 - 930 = 70 cm is left. (c) 70 cm = 0.7 m = 700 mm.
s: (a) Converts 1.25 m to 125 cm and finds 750 + 180 = 930 cm
(b) Converts 10 m to 1000 cm and finds 70 cm left
(c) Writes 70 cm as 0.7 m and 700 mm

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The thickness of a page of a book is more conveniently written in millimetres than in kilometres.
Reason (R): The SI unit of length is the metre, and its symbol is m.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A classroom ceiling is 3.1 m above the floor. A fan hangs from the ceiling on a down-rod, and the fan body below the rod is 20 cm deep, with the blades at the bottom of the body. The electrician has three down-rods: 40 cm, 600 mm and 0.85 m long. For safety the blades must be at least 2.3 m above the floor, and the school wants them as low as is safe. (a) Write the three rod lengths in centimetres. (b) Find how high above the floor the blades would be with each rod. (c) Which rods are safe? (d) Which rod should the electrician fit? Give the blade height in millimetres.
questions.a: (a) 40 cm, 60 cm and 85 cm. (b) The ceiling is 310 cm high: 310 - 40 - 20 = 250 cm; 310 - 60 - 20 = 230 cm; 310 - 85 - 20 = 205 cm. (c) The 40 cm rod (2.5 m) and the 600 mm rod (exactly 2.3 m) are safe; the 0.85 m rod (2.05 m) is not. (d) The 600 mm rod, because it gives the lowest safe height; the blades are then 2300 mm above the floor.
s: (a) Converts the rods to 40 cm, 60 cm and 85 cm
(b) Finds blade heights of 250 cm, 230 cm and 205 cm from a 310 cm ceiling
(c) Names the 40 cm and 600 mm rods as safe and rejects 0.85 m
(d) Chooses the 600 mm rod and gives 2300 mm

questions.q: Neha is making a fact card about her day. Write each length in the unit asked. (a) Her school is 3 km from her home: write it in metres. (b) Her desk is 1.2 m long: write it in centimetres. (c) Her pencil is 150 mm long: write it in centimetres. (d) Her eraser is 4 cm long: write it in millimetres. (e) The school's walking track is 2000 m long: write it in kilometres.
s: (d) 4 cm = 40 mm

questions.q: Rahul writes in his notebook, '2.5 km = 250 m'. What is his mistake?
questions.a: He used 1 km = 100 m; the correct value is 2500 m.
o: He used 1 km = 100 m; the correct value is 2500 m.
He made no mistake; 2.5 km is the same as 250 m.
He should have divided by 1000; the correct value is 0.0025 m.
He used 1 km = 100 m; the correct value is 25000 m.

questions.q: Where should your eye be when you read the position of a pencil's tip on a scale?
questions.a: Directly above the tip of the pencil
o: Directly above the tip of the pencil
A little to the left of the tip
A little to the right of the tip
At any angle, if the scale touches the pencil

questions.q: Which is the correct way to place a scale to measure the length of a book?
questions.a: Along the length of the book, in contact with its edge
o: Along the length of the book, in contact with its edge
Tilted, so that only one end of the scale touches the book
Held a little above the book so the marks are easy to see
Across the width of the book, in contact with its edge

questions.q: The zero end of Ravi's 15-cm scale is broken. He places one end of a matchbox at the 2.0 cm mark, and the other end of the matchbox is at the 6.8 cm mark. (a) What must he do with the two readings? (b) What is the length of the matchbox?
questions.a: (a) He must subtract the reading at the starting mark (2.0 cm) from the reading at the other end (6.8 cm). (b) 6.8 cm - 2.0 cm = 4.8 cm.
s: (a) Says the starting reading is subtracted from the reading at the other end
(b) Finds 4.8 cm

questions.q: Gita measures the height of her study table with a 15-cm scale, placing it again and again up the table leg, and gets 76.4 cm. Her brother holds a metre scale upright against the same leg in one placement and gets 75.6 cm. (a) Whose result is more likely to be correct? (b) Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Her brother's result (75.6 cm). (b) A metre scale is the appropriate scale for this length and covers it in one placement; the 15-cm scale has to be moved several times, and any small gap or overlap at each move adds an error.
s: (a) Chooses the brother's metre-scale reading
(b) Explains that the 15-cm scale is moved several times, adding error at each move, while the metre scale needs one placement

questions.q:
Assertion (A): While reading a scale, the eye can be placed at any angle, as long as the scale touches the object.
Reason (R): The eye should be directly above the mark that is being read.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: The 0 mark of Karan's 15-cm scale has worn away. To measure a crayon, he holds the scale a little above the crayon, lines up one end of the crayon with the 1.0 cm mark and sees the other end in line with the 8.2 cm mark. He writes 'Crayon = 8.2 cm'. (a) What is wrong with the way he held the scale? (b) What is wrong with his answer? (c) Write the correct length of the crayon.
questions.a: (a) The scale must be placed in contact with the crayon along its length, not held above it. (b) He started from the 1.0 cm mark, so he must subtract 1.0 cm from the reading at the other end; he wrote the end reading as the length. (c) 8.2 cm - 1.0 cm = 7.2 cm.
s: (a) Says the scale should touch the crayon along its length
(b) Says the 1.0 cm starting reading was not subtracted
(c) Finds 7.2 cm

questions.q: A carpenter's helper measures a window frame so that a glass pane can be cut to fit it exactly. His wooden scale has its first 2 cm chipped off. Along the width, one edge of the frame is at the 2.0 cm mark and the other edge is at the 64.5 cm mark. Along the height, one edge is at the 5.0 cm mark and the other edge is at the 47.3 cm mark. He orders a pane 64.5 cm wide and 47.3 cm high. (a) What is the true width of the frame? (b) What is the true height of the frame? (c) By how many millimetres is the ordered pane too wide, and by how many too high? (d) Will the ordered pane fit the frame? Give a reason. (e) What single mistake did the helper make, and what is the correct method?
questions.a: (a) 64.5 cm - 2.0 cm = 62.5 cm. (b) 47.3 cm - 5.0 cm = 42.3 cm. (c) Too wide by 2.0 cm = 20 mm and too high by 5.0 cm = 50 mm. (d) No; the pane is larger than the frame in both directions, so it will not go in. (e) He wrote the reading at the far edge as the length without subtracting the reading at the starting mark; with a broken scale, subtract the starting reading from the reading at the other end.
s: (a) Finds the width 62.5 cm
(b) Finds the height 42.3 cm
(c) Finds 20 mm too wide and 50 mm too high
(d) Says the pane will not fit because it is larger both ways
(e) Names the missing subtraction of the starting reading as the mistake and states the correct method

questions.q: (a) Name an instrument suitable for measuring the height of a room. (b) Why is a 15-cm scale not convenient for measuring the height of a room? (c) Name a scale suitable for measuring the length of your pencil.
questions.a: (a) A metre scale or a measuring tape. (b) The height of a room is many times longer than 15 cm, so the small scale would have to be moved again and again. (c) A 15-cm scale.
s: (a) Names a metre scale or measuring tape
(b) Explains that the room is far longer than 15 cm, so the scale must be moved many times
(c) Names a 15-cm scale

questions.q: True or False? 'A metre scale is the most suitable instrument for measuring the size of a person's chest.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. A chest is curved and a rigid metre scale cannot measure it directly; a flexible measuring tape, such as a tailor's tape, is more suitable.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the chest is curved, so a flexible tape such as a tailor's tape is used, not a rigid metre scale

questions.q: The zero end of Mitali's 15-cm scale is broken, so she uses the 1.0 cm mark as her starting mark. A ribbon is longer than the scale. She puts one end of the ribbon at the 1.0 cm mark and makes a pencil mark on the ribbon at the 15.0 cm mark. She then moves the scale so that her pencil mark is at the 1.0 cm mark, and the other end of the ribbon is at the 8.5 cm mark. How long is the ribbon?
Which of these can be used to measure the length of a curved line drawn on paper?
questions.a: A thread

questions.q: Ali lays a thread exactly along a curved line and marks the thread where the line ends. What should he do next to find the length of the curved line?
questions.a: Straighten the thread and measure the marked length on a scale
o: Straighten the thread and measure the marked length on a scale
Measure the straight gap between the two ends of the curved line
Count the number of bends the thread made along the line
Measure the thread with a metre scale while it lies on the curve

questions.q: Why are some length-measuring devices made of flexible materials? Give one example of such a device and one length it is used to measure.
questions.a: A flexible device can bend to follow a curved surface or line, which a rigid scale cannot do. Example: a tailor's measuring tape, used to measure the size of a person's chest (or the girth of a tree).
s: Explains that a flexible device bends along a curved surface, which a rigid scale cannot
Gives an example such as a tailor's tape with a use such as chest size or the girth of a tree

questions.q: Riya wants to find the length of a curved river drawn on a map in her atlas. (a) What should she lay along the curved river? (b) What should she do at the point where the river ends? (c) After straightening, the marked part of the thread starts at the 0 mark of her scale and ends at the 18.6 cm mark. What is the length of the river on the map?
questions.a: (a) A thread, laid exactly along the curve (or a flexible measuring tape). (b) Mark the thread at that point, then straighten the thread along a scale. (c) 18.6 cm.
s: (a) Lays a thread (or flexible tape) exactly along the curve
(b) Marks the thread at the end point before straightening it
(c) Reads the length as 18.6 cm

questions.q:
Read these statements about measuring a curved line.
I. A rigid metre scale cannot be bent to follow a curved line.
II. A thread laid along a curved line is marked where the line ends before it is straightened.
III. The straight gap between the two ends of a curved line is equal to the length of the curved line.
Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A thread can be used to measure the length of a curved line.
Reason (R): The smallest length that can be measured with an ordinary 15-cm scale is 1 mm.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
For the school's Annual Day, three curved flower beds will each be edged with one unbroken piece of lace. The gardener lays a thread along the curved edge of each bed, marks it, straightens it and measures it: Bed A needs 2.35 m, Bed B needs 1.8 m and Bed C needs 245 cm. The shop sells lace in rolls of 5 m at Rs 60 a roll, and in rolls of 3.5 m at Rs 45 a roll. The school will buy only one kind of roll. A piece for one bed may be cut from any roll, but two pieces cannot be joined.
(a) Why did the gardener use a thread and not a metre scale on the beds?
(b) Write the length needed for Bed C in metres.
(c) Find the total length of lace needed for the three beds.
(d) Which kind of roll should the school buy, and how many, to spend the least? Show your working.
questions.a: (a) The edges are curved; a rigid metre scale cannot follow a curve, but a thread can be laid along it and then straightened and measured. (b) 245 cm = 2.45 m. (c) 2.35 + 1.80 + 2.45 = 6.60 m. (d) Rolls of 5 m: Beds A and C (2.35 + 2.45 = 4.80 m) fit in one roll and Bed B (1.8 m) in a second, so 2 rolls cost Rs 120. Rolls of 3.5 m: no two beds fit in one roll (the smallest pair, A and B, needs 4.15 m), so 3 rolls are needed, costing Rs 135. The school should buy two 5 m rolls.
s: (a) Explains that a rigid scale cannot follow the curved edge, so a thread is laid along it
(b) Converts 245 cm to 2.45 m
(c) Finds the total 6.60 m
(d) Shows two 5 m rolls (Rs 120) against three 3.5 m rolls (Rs 135) and chooses the 5 m rolls

questions.q: True or False? 'A flexible measuring tape can be laid directly along a curved line to measure its length.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. A flexible measuring tape bends and follows the curve, so the length of a curved line can be read from it directly, just as a thread can be used.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: a flexible tape bends to follow the curve, so the curved length can be read from it

questions.q: A craftswoman in Jaipur decorates the outer edge of bangles with gold thread, going once around each bangle. She lays a cotton thread once around a medium bangle, marks it, straightens it and finds that 20.4 cm of gold thread is needed for one medium bangle. Her spool holds 5 m of gold thread. (a) Why did she use a cotton thread and not a 15-cm scale to find the length? (b) Write the length of gold thread on the spool in centimetres. (c) How many medium bangles can she decorate fully from one spool, and how much gold thread is left over? (d) A small bangle needs 18.8 cm. Can she decorate a small bangle with the leftover thread?
questions.a: (a) The edge of a bangle is curved; a rigid scale cannot follow it, but a thread can be wound along it and then straightened and measured. (b) 5 m = 500 cm. (c) 500 / 20.4 gives 24 bangles, using 24 x 20.4 = 489.6 cm, so 500 - 489.6 = 10.4 cm is left. (d) No, because 10.4 cm is less than the 18.8 cm needed.
s: (a) Explains that the curved edge needs a thread, not a rigid scale
(b) Converts 5 m to 500 cm
(c) Finds 24 bangles and 10.4 cm left over
(d) Compares 10.4 cm with 18.8 cm and says no

questions.q: Sohan wants the length of the curved edge of a semicircular table top. He says, 'The curved edge and the straight edge join the same two corners, so I only need to measure the straight edge with a metre scale.' (a) Is he right? (b) Give a reason. (c) Describe how he should measure the curved edge.
questions.a: (a) No. (b) The curved edge bends outwards between the two corners, so it is longer than the straight edge; equal end points do not mean equal lengths. (c) Lay a thread (or a flexible tape) exactly along the curved edge, mark the thread where the edge ends, straighten it and measure the marked length with a metre scale.
s: (a) Verdict: No
(b) Explains that the curved edge is longer than the straight edge joining the same corners
(c) Describes laying, marking, straightening and measuring a thread (or using a flexible tape)

questions.q: When a distance is stated with respect to a fixed object or point, what is that point called?
questions.a: A reference point

questions.q: On a highway, a kilometre stone reads 'Mysuru 45 km'. What is the reference point here?
questions.a: Mysuru

questions.q: Raju says the town hospital is 3 km away. Seema says the same hospital is 5 km away. Both have measured correctly. (a) How can both of them be right? (b) What should each of them add to the statement so that everyone understands it?
questions.a: (a) They are measuring the distance from different points, for example from their own houses. (b) Each should name the reference point, such as '3 km from my house', or both should use the same fixed point, such as the bus stand.
s: (a) Explains that they measured from different points (different reference points)
(b) Says each must state the reference point, or both must use one common fixed point

questions.q: True or False? 'A snail crawling slowly up a wall is at rest, because it is moving so slowly.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The snail's position changes with respect to the wall (the reference point) with time, so it is in motion, however slowly it moves.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: its position changes with respect to the wall with time, so it is in motion; slowness does not matter

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A passenger sitting on a seat in a moving bus is at rest with respect to the bus.
Reason (R): The passenger's position does not change with respect to the bus with time.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Kiran sits in her seat in a moving train. Her bag lies on the rack above her and does not slide. Which statement about the bag is correct?
questions.a: It is at rest with respect to Kiran and in motion with respect to a tree outside.
o: It is at rest with respect to Kiran and in motion with respect to a tree outside.
It is in motion with respect to Kiran and at rest with respect to a tree outside.
It is at rest with respect to both Kiran and a tree outside.
It is in motion with respect to both Kiran and a tree outside.

questions.q: (a) When is an object said to be in motion? (b) When is an object said to be at rest? (c) A bicycle stands parked at the school gate all day. Taking the gate as the reference point, is the bicycle at rest or in motion?
questions.a: (a) When its position changes with respect to a reference point with time. (b) When its position does not change with respect to the reference point with time. (c) At rest, because its position with respect to the gate does not change.
s: (a) Motion: position changes with respect to a reference point with time
(b) Rest: position does not change with respect to the reference point with time
(c) Says the bicycle is at rest with respect to the gate

questions.q: Meena sits in a moving train next to her father. A tea seller walks down the aisle of her coach. Outside, a cow stands still in a field. On the next track, another train moves in the same direction at exactly the same pace, so that the same window of that train stays opposite Meena. (a) Is Meena at rest or in motion with respect to her father? Give a reason. (b) Is Meena at rest or in motion with respect to the cow? Give a reason. (c) Is the other train at rest or in motion with respect to Meena? (d) Is the tea seller at rest or in motion with respect to Meena? (e) Meena's brother asks, 'Is Meena moving or not?' Explain why this question cannot be answered without naming a reference point.
questions.a: (a) At rest, because her position with respect to her father does not change with time. (b) In motion, because her position with respect to the cow changes with time. (c) At rest, because its position with respect to Meena does not change (the same window stays opposite her). (d) In motion, because his position with respect to Meena changes as he walks. (e) Whether an object is at rest or in motion depends on the reference point: Meena is at rest with respect to her father and the other train but in motion with respect to the cow, so the answer changes with the reference point chosen.
s: (a) At rest with respect to her father, with the reason
(b) In motion with respect to the cow, with the reason
(c) The other train is at rest with respect to Meena
(d) The tea seller is in motion with respect to Meena
(e) Explains that rest or motion depends on the reference point, using two of the answers above

questions.q:
A cycle rally is held on a long straight road. The organisers measure every position from the start banner. Water points are set up at 2 km, 5 km and 9 km from the start banner, in that order along the road. A volunteer at Water Point 2 phones in: 'A cyclist has stopped 3 km beyond me, farther from the start.'
(a) How far apart are Water Point 2 and Water Point 3?
(b) How far from the start banner has the cyclist stopped?
(c) Which water point is nearest to the stopped cyclist, and how far away is it?
(d) Should every volunteer report positions from the start banner, or from their own water point? Give a reason for your choice.
questions.a: (a) 9 km - 5 km = 4 km. (b) 5 km + 3 km = 8 km from the start banner. (c) Water Point 3, which is 9 - 8 = 1 km away (Water Point 2 is 3 km away). (d) From the start banner: with one common reference point every report means the same thing and can be compared at once on the organisers' list. A report from a water point is correct only if the water point is named, and it must then be converted, as in (b), which takes time and can cause mistakes.
s: (a) Finds 4 km between Water Points 2 and 3
(b) Finds 8 km from the start banner
(c) Names Water Point 3 at 1 km
(d) Chooses one common reference point (the start banner) and explains why reports then agree

questions.q:
At a mela in Rohtak, Arjun visits four rides. On the merry-go-round, the wooden horses turn round and round at a steady pace. On the cradle ride, the seats hang from a tall frame and rock to and fro about the frame again and again. On the water slide, a child slides once down a straight slope into a pool. On the toy train, the train runs round and round a circular track at a steady pace.
(a) Which two rides show circular motion?
(b) Which ride shows oscillatory motion?
(c) Which ride shows linear motion?
(d) Which rides show periodic motion? Why is the water slide not one of them?
questions.a: (a) The merry-go-round and the toy train. (b) The cradle ride. (c) The water slide. (d) The merry-go-round, the toy train and the cradle ride, because each repeats its path after a fixed interval of time. The child on the slide goes down the straight slope only once and does not repeat the path.
s: (a) Names the merry-go-round and the toy train
(b) Names the cradle ride
(c) Names the water slide
(d) Names the three repeating rides as periodic and says the slide does not repeat its path

questions.q: Name the type of motion in each case. (a) A lift going straight up from the ground floor to the third floor. (b) A point on the edge of a potter's wheel as the wheel turns.

s: (a) Linear motion
(b) Circular motion

questions.q:

II. The free end of a metal strip pressed to a table, pushed slightly and released, shows oscillatory motion.
III. A swing moving to and fro shows linear motion.
Which of these is/are correct?
questions.a: II only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The motion of a merry-go-round turning at a steady pace is periodic.
Reason (R): Only to-and-fro motion can be periodic.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: Tarun says, 'Every motion that repeats itself is circular motion.' Check his claim using two examples: an eraser tied to a thread and whirled round in a circle, and a swing moving to and fro.
questions.a: Tarun is not right. The whirled eraser moves along a circular path again and again, so it is circular and repeats. But the swing also repeats its motion while moving to and fro about a fixed position, which is oscillatory motion, not circular. So repeating (periodic) motion can be circular or oscillatory.
s: Verdict: the claim is wrong
Shows that the whirled eraser is circular and repeats its path
Shows that the swing repeats but is oscillatory, so repeating motion is not always circular

questions.q: In a village, Rekha watches four things: (i) a pair of bullocks walking round and round a fixed post at a steady pace to turn a sugarcane crusher; (ii) a man working a hand pump at a steady pace, whose handle moves up and down about the pin that holds it; (iii) a bullock cart moving once along a straight village road; (iv) a coconut falling straight down from a tree. (a) Name the type of motion of (i) and of (ii). (b) Name the type of motion of (iii) and of (iv). (c) Which of the four show periodic motion? Give the reason. (d) The bullocks are then untied and walk straight to their shed. What type of motion do they now show, and is it periodic? (e) Rekha says, 'The pump handle and the coconut both move downwards, so they show the same type of motion.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: (a) (i) Circular motion; (ii) oscillatory motion. (b) (iii) and (iv) are both linear motion. (c) (i) and (ii), because each repeats its path after a fixed interval of time: the bullocks go round the same circle again and again, and the handle moves to and fro again and again. (d) Linear motion, and it is not periodic because the path is not repeated. (e) No. The handle moves to and fro about a fixed position (the pin), so it is oscillatory; the coconut moves once along a straight line, so it is linear.
s: (a) Circular for the bullocks and oscillatory for the pump handle
(b) Linear for both the cart and the coconut
(c) Names (i) and (ii) as periodic because they repeat their path after a fixed interval
(d) Linear and not periodic
(e) Says no: the handle is oscillatory about the pin, the coconut is linear

questions.q: Which observation is enough to say that the motion of an object is periodic?
questions.a: It repeats its path after a fixed interval of time.
o: It repeats its path after a fixed interval of time.
It moves along a curved path.
It changes the direction in which it moves.
Its position changes with respect to a reference point.

questions.q: In a science class, the teacher shows three marbles. Marble P is released from the inner edge of a round steel bowl and rolls to and fro across the bottom, about the lowest point of the bowl. Marble Q is rolled once along a straight groove on a ruler. Marble R is pushed inside a ring-shaped tray and goes round and round along the ring. (a) Name the type of motion of each marble. (b) Which marbles repeat their path, and which one does not? (c) Sonu says, 'Marble P shows circular motion because the bowl is round.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: (a) P: oscillatory motion; Q: linear motion; R: circular motion. (b) P and R repeat their paths (P moves to and fro again and again, R goes round the ring again and again); Q moves along the groove only once and does not. (c) No. The shape of the bowl does not decide the type of motion; the path does. Marble P does not go round a circular path; it moves to and fro about a fixed position (the lowest point), so its motion is oscillatory.
s: (a) Names P oscillatory, Q linear and R circular
(b) Says P and R repeat their paths and Q does not
(c) Says Sonu is wrong because P moves to and fro about the lowest point, not along a circular path
